hero.title: Earth Data Board
hero.sub1: The second piece of "one sky, one ground"—
hero.sub2: watches the sky; this one watches the ground: the planet's pulse beneath, city environments on the surface, and the full-disk Earth imaged from the Sun–Earth L1 point.

footer: All data come from free public APIs (EMSC / NASA EPIC / NASA EONET / Open-Meteo / NOAA GML / NASA GISTEMP / NSIDC / USGS HANS / NOAA tsunami.gov) and are for science outreach and visualization only. Earthquake parameters are automatic initial estimates, subject to revision by the China Earthquake Networks Center or USGS; environmental data are model interpolations, not station measurements; greenhouse-gas and temperature-anomaly figures are upstream monthly updates. Volcano and tsunami levels are official operational judgements; in emergencies follow instructions from local governments and emergency-management authorities.

m.quake24hInfo: Global count of earthquakes magnitude 2.5+ in the past 24 hours (USGS global network; micro-quakes below threshold excluded).
m.maxMagInfo: The strongest earthquake within 24h; M5+ may cause damage, M6+ is a major quake.
m.maxDepthInfo: The deepest earthquake within 24h; deep quakes occur within subducting slabs and usually feel weak at the surface.
m.co2Info: NOAA global monthly-mean CO₂ (parts per million by volume); about 278 ppm before industrialization.
m.ch4Info: Global monthly-mean methane (parts per billion by volume); about 722 ppb before industrialization, 28× the warming potential of CO₂ over a century.
m.tempAnomalyInfo: NASA GISTEMP land–ocean temperature deviation from the 1951–1980 baseline; the Paris Agreement aims to hold warming within +1.5 °C.
m.arcticIceInfo: NSIDC Arctic sea-ice extent (minimum month is September each year), a classic climate-change indicator.
m.pm25Info: Arithmetic mean of PM2.5 across 5 sample cities (Beijing/Shanghai/Guangzhou/Chengdu/Lhasa), not a national average.
m.volcanoInfo: Count of U.S. volcanoes above the USGS HANS "normal" level; the bracket is the number at orange or above (truly active).
m.tsunamiInfo: Bulletins at "advisory" or above from NOAA's two tsunami warning centers; most others are information statements ruling out a threat.

strong.caption: M5.5+ quakes in {days} days, aggregated by UTC calendar day (EMSC) · redder means more strong quakes that day

epic.title: DSCOVR/EPIC full-disk Earth
epic.source: NASA EPIC (epic.gsfc.nasa.gov), imaged from the Sun–Earth L1 point, about one frame every 2 hours
epic.note: The EPIC camera continuously stares at Earth's sunlit face from the Sun–Earth L1 point, combining 10 narrow bands into natural color—the most classic "sky looking down at ground" view.

eonet.aria: Global natural events in the past 30 days
eonet.mapTitle: Natural events in the past 30 days
eonet.mapSource: NASA EONET (eonet.gsfc.nasa.gov), ongoing natural events, refreshed hourly
eonet.listSource: NASA EONET; click an event title to open its official page
eonet.legendNote: Only ongoing events with locatable coordinates are shown

climate.envSource: Open-Meteo (no key), one multi-city call each for weather and air quality, refreshed every 10 min; AQI is European standard
climate.ghgTitle: The greenhouse-gas trio: CO₂ / CH₄ / N₂O
climate.ghgSource: NOAA GML (gml.noaa.gov) global baseline monthly mean, deseasonalized trend, refreshed every 12h
climate.tempSource: NASA GISTEMP v4 (data.giss.nasa.gov), land–ocean, baseline 1951–1980, refreshed every 12h
climate.iceSource: NSIDC sea-ice index (noaadata.apps.nsidc.org), extreme month per pole: Arctic September, Antarctic February

temp.caption: Global land–ocean temperature anomaly (NASA GISTEMP v4, baseline {baseline}) · warmest year {warmestYear} (+{warmestAnom} °C) · {lastYear} +{lastAnom} °C · latest 12-mo mean +{latest12} °C — the Paris Agreement aims to hold warming within +1.5 °C

seaIce.caption: {zh} {month} sea-ice extent (extreme month, NSIDC) · 1981–1990 mean {avg1980s} (cold line) vs 2011–2020 mean {avg2010s} (warm line) · vs {year} {word} {decline}%

co2.caption: Global monthly mean CO₂ over 5 years (NOAA global ocean boundary-layer average) · annual growth ~{growth} ppm — pre-industrial level was about 280 ppm, current growth is mainly driven by fossil-fuel emissions

air.title: City air quality
air.source: Open-Meteo Air Quality (European CAMS model output, EU-standard AQI)
air.lead: PM2.5 are particles ≤2.5 µm that reach the alveoli and enter the blood, the top indicator of air-quality standards worldwide; PM10 include coarser dust affecting mainly the upper airways.
air.leadAvg: Current {count}-city average PM2.5 is about {val} µg/m³.
air.aqiHeaderTip: European Environment Agency (EAQI) standard. Breakpoints differ from China's AQI, but share the same bands as the glossary.

wx.title: City weather now
wx.source: Open-Meteo Forecast (WMO 4677 weather codes), refreshed every 10 min
wx.lead: Sorted from highest to lowest current temperature.
wx.leadTemp: North–south temperature gap now is about {delta}°C ({hot} {hott}°C vs {cold} {coldt}°C).
wx.leadFeel: "Feels-like" temperature combines humidity and wind, closer to human perception than dry-bulb temperature.

archive.title: Climate archive (last decade)
archive.source: Open-Meteo Archive · ERA5 reanalysis daily values, aggregated to yearly means server-side
archive.lead: Bar length is scaled to the lowest–highest decadal mean temperature: blue is cooler, red is warmer. Having warm and cool years is normal year-to-year noise (ENSO, monsoon strength, etc.); what matters is the difference between the two ends of the decade: a single-station rise of {delta}°C over ten years already exceeds the interannual noise.

volcano.noaaSource: NOAA tsunami.gov (Pacific center PHEB + national center PAAQ)
volcano.emptyVol: None of the three USGS observatories has a volcano above "normal" right now—good news
volcano.emptyTsu: Neither warning center currently has a valid bulletin
volcano.prose: Color code and alert level are not the same: the code only cares whether ash reaches aircraft, the alert level cares whether residents face lava flows and pyroclastic flows. A quiet effusive eruption can be "ground warning + green code", while a low but sustained ash column can be "orange code + ground alert".
volcano.whyP1: Tsunamis are triggered by vertical seafloor displacement—strike-slip quakes (faults sliding horizontally) barely push water, so an M7.5 strike-slip can carry zero tsunami risk while an M7.0 thrust quake raises several-meter walls. The warning center must judge fault type, focal depth and seafloor displacement within minutes; that conclusion is the bulletin level.
volcano.whyP2: So an "information statement" is not hand-waving—it dissolves a false alarm in advance: it states clearly "a quake happened, but it will not raise a tsunami." Only a handful worldwide escalate to "warning" each year.
volcano.whyP3: Another counter-intuitive point: deep-ocean tsunamis can have wavelengths of hundreds of km but heights of only tens of cm, often unnoticed on ships. They travel at √(g·h)—about 700–800 km/h at 4000 m depth, near jet-cruise speed; entering shallow water they drop to tens of km/h as energy is forced upward, becoming the wall at the shore. Abnormal seawater retreat is the signal minutes before arrival.

case.turkeyDesc: Two large quakes ruptured along two near-parallel faults within a single day; shallow depth + dense population + poor seismic resilience combined to kill over 50,000 across both countries. It illustrates the board's two core dimensions: magnitude sets the energy scale (M7.8 is already a great quake), while depth decides how much of that energy reaches the surface — at the same magnitude, a deep quake usually feels far weaker on the ground.
case.tongaDesc: Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai is a submarine volcano whose eruption triggered a transoceanic tsunami; even Peru, 10,000 km away, suffered an oil spill from abnormal surge. This case links the Volcano Alert and Tsunami Bulletin tabs: a submarine volcano can not only erupt but also excite a tsunami like an undersea quake — and is even harder to warn against.
case.tohokuDesc: The Pacific Plate snapped back while subducting at the Japan Trench, releasing energy equivalent to thousands of atomic bombs. The huge tsunami overtopped seawalls and caused the Fukushima Daiichi accident. It reminds us that the board's 24h earthquakes are only the tip of the iceberg: true mega-quakes come from subduction zones, and the destruction mostly stems from the accompanying tsunami rather than the shaking itself.
case.turkeyMagInfo: Strike-slip rupture on the East Anatolian Fault; the board's M6+ strong-quake red band
case.depthShallow: Shallow: energy reaches the surface directly, large damage radius
case.turkeyAftershockInfo: Occurred on another fault segment about 9 hours after the mainshock
case.tongaPlumeInfo: Pierced the tropopause into the stratosphere; one of the strongest eruptions in recent years
case.tongaTsunamiInfo: Triggered by caldera collapse; 1m+ surges recorded in Japan and the Americas
case.aviationTop: The highest aviation alert level on the board's volcano page
case.tohokuMagInfo: Mega-thrust at the subduction zone; among the largest magnitudes ever observed
case.tohokuDepthInfo: Sudden slip of the shallow locked patch on the plate interface
case.tohokuRunupInfo: Miyagi/Iwate coast, far beyond the tsunami warning benchmark
